note: Uru-inimgina’s "reforms" read as evidence of royal levies in Lagaš (Diakonoff’s reading, reported by Yoffee).

note: Yoffee (p. 290) rejects Steinkeller’s view that private land ownership in the south was insignificant.

A recent reexamination of the sources has shown that the economy of Lagash was in fact controlled by the king through the intermediary of large domains connected with the temples of the city’s prominent deities.

shg_comment: These reforms would actually be an interesting situation to consider if visible in the tablet VAE or H/W or other elements studied in the paper.

note: The crown works through temple domains rather than a separate palace sector.

quote: Les dates évoquent, par le choix des événements éponymes, les divers domaines de l’activité royale : la diplomatie, principalement le va-et-vient de messagers entre la Susiane et la Babylonie
note: Haft Tepe year names of king Tepti-ahar.

quote: trois autres portent celle du sceau d’Athibu, gouverneur de Kabnak et confident de ce roi
note: Kabnak (Haft Tepe) governed for the king of Susa and Anšan.

quote: Au total, ce ne sont pas moins de cinquante-cinq documents, sur un total d’environ 400 pièces dépouillées, qui font mention de Tepti-ahar ou d’Athibu.
note: The archive: lists of persons, livestock, textiles, metals and goldwork, some legal documents, and school, lexical and scholarly texts; Tepti-ahar’s seal impressed at least 14 times.

quote: In the course of the Middle Elamite period, Elam became one of the most important political powers in the region. Its political and economic rise was mirrored by a certain cultural self-confidence.
note: Kings of "Susa and Anšan" rule lowland Susiana and highland Fars; the Shutrukids take Babylonia in the 12th century (p. 236).

quote: It was only in the Middle Elamite period that the kings who unified lowland and highland for nearly four centuries celebrated their deeds as great builders with inscriptions, mainly in Susiana.
note: Royal inscriptions as evidence of a lowland-highland kingdom.

quote: In the early phase of the Middle Elamite period, different cities were governed by local authorities who were also named EŠŠANA (“king”). In tablets from Haft Tappeh, such regional governors are mentioned for Huhnur, Anshan, and Halisrati during the reign of Tepti-ahar
note: Local rulers and a šaknu (Athibu of Kabnak) under the king of Susa and Anšan; the same page says supremacy seems "concentrated in the hand of the king alone".

quote: All the corpora examined above seems to pertain to a relatively local scope, for example, they are not concerned with the administration of far provinces.
note: No written evidence for provincial administration from Haft Tappeh, Malyan or Susa.

quote: Compared to other elite seals, that of Tepti-ahar was evidently used more often for administrative purposes, obviously in order to maintain full control over the government
note: Royal seal dominates the Haft Tappeh administration; a cattle record is added to the "big tablet of the king".

quote: 46 oxen of Ishepiltirra, 30 oxen of Tashritu – total: 76 oxen, administrative responsibility of Atta-Napir which the king investigates and adds to the royal cumulative record (lit. ‘big tablet of the king’)
note: Inference: royal accounting of herds held by officials (Beckman 1991). No tax archive is known, so the score is weak.

quote: Of particular note is the lack of other text types such as legal or administrative documents in both this and the previous ME II period. It is unclear whether this is the result of chance or reflects a reduced utilization of writing in the social organization and everyday life in these phases.
note: After Haft Tappeh (ME I) there is no administrative writing except Malyan c. 1000.

quote: Textual evidence points to a well-organized administration system controlled by the king. All deliveries of raw materials and objects seem to have been registered by special officials, named puhu-teppu.
note: Haft Tappeh, reigns of Tepti-ahar and Inšušinak-šar-ili.

quote: The city was conceived as a sacred center in which different temples of various Elamite deities were planned.
note: Al-Untaš-Napiriša (Chogha Zanbil), a royal foundation with ziqqurrat and temples; Untaš-Napiriša equips the temples with statues and stelae (p. 242). Evidence is royal building, not temple administration.

quote: cultic provisions are known from Persepolis (see Henkelman, Chapter 39 in this volume) and temple institutions are probably mentioned in the Susa Acropolis tablets.
note: No Middle Elamite temple archive shows how temples were run.

quote: Textual sources do not allow for the illumination of the quotidian in the Middle Elamite era. In the absence of private documents like those available for the sukkalmah era, the social and economic nature of everyday urban life remains to be charted.
note: Exception: the Malamir legal texts (p. 237).

quote: In the formulaic oath in sukkalmah legal tablets, for example, usually the king (sukkalmah), viceroy (sukkal of Elam), and sometimes even governor of Susa (sukkal of Susa) are cited, while in the Middle Elamite period “Malamir” tablets only the king was invoked.
note: Royal oath in legal documents; no law collection. p. 237: neither Haft Tappeh nor Susa gives legal texts on everyday judicial problems.

quote: The onomasticon is mostly Elamite; month-names are also Elamite (Herrero 1976: 93–94). Some texts are dated internally with day, month-name, and year-name.
note: Haft Tappeh year names refer to royal acts (cf. Glassner 1991 p. 112).

quote: the indication of the month without year (e.g. in the Malyan EDD tablets and in the Susa Acropolis tablets), reflects an archive having a limited scope in time
note: Late Middle Elamite Malyan tablets carry no year.

quote: Numerous school tablets were discovered at Susa and also in smaller quantities at Haft Tappeh/Kabnak, Abu Fandowa (Herrero and Glassner 1996: 75–82) and perhaps in Anshan/Tall-e Malyan.
note: Glassner adds that apprentices of both languages attended the same schools (D’Erme 1990).

quote: the narrow link between administration and scribal school could be emphasized, confirming that the school trained scribes to write both administrative and literary documents, or that administration training included the literary curriculum.
note: Conditional: find-spots of the Haft Tappeh tablets are unpublished.

quote: Il en va de même pour le millier de textes administratifs qui a été retrouvé à Isin et documente les ateliers d'artisanat de la capitale pendant trente-trois ans (de l'an 4 d'Išbi-Erra à l'an 3 de Šu-ilišu).
note: Palace craft workshops of Isin continue Ur III practice; cf. Van De Mieroop 1987.

quote: Inscriptions commémoratives, hymnes royaux, code de lois (Lipit-Eštar), correspondance royale sont - et se veulent - les continuateurs de la tradition néo-sumérienne de la troisième dynastie d'Ur
note: Isin presents itself as continuing Ur III administrative and scribal tradition.

quote: It seems, however, that this workshop was under the control of the palace, especially since many of its products are destined for the palace and are used as official presents for other countries. The many connections between the date formulae and the records of the workshop also suggest royal control.
note: Isin craft archive, 920 texts, Išbi-Erra to Šu-ilišu. Van De Mieroop notes that no official title links the staff to the palace with certainty, so palace control is an inference.

quote: The documents of the Isin archive show a continuation of the traditions of the Ur III period; the language and the format of the texts are the same as in the preceding period.
note: Direct statement on tablet format: Early Isin administrative records keep the Ur III format. Sealed receipts with receiving and certifying officials (p. 117).

quote: whereas in the craft archive from Ur under Ibbi-Sin the craftsmen are recorded active every day, in the Isin archive the records indicate that they were only present fifty percent of the time. This may be an indication of the growing role of private enterprise in the early second millennium.
note: Tentative ("may be"): the first sign of private enterprise beside institutional labour. [Rescored by ShG, 8 Nov, from 1 to 2.]

quote: Land was rented, bought, and sold in the north (31, 101, 108, 252) and property was accumulated, inherited, and disputed in both north and south
note: p. 298: entrepreneurial middlemen supply palaces and temples (Van De Mieroop on Ur copper).

quote: In the Babylonian south after the collapse of Ur, no supreme political power ruled in the land.
note: Isin and Larsa compete for Nippur; Kish symbolizes rather than exercises control in the north.

quote: in the 19th regnal year of Išbi-Erra (1993/2 BCE), peaceful relations still prevailed between him and Elam, as one can infer from the presence of messengers of Kindattu and of another Elamite ruler, Idaddu, in Isin.
note: Only diplomatic messengers are recorded in the Isin administrative texts; no royal courier or road-station system is described for Isin or early Larsa.

quote: Like Išbi-Erra, Išme-Dagān also appointed priests in the temples of various Mesopotamian cities: the priestess of the god Ninurta in Nippur, the priestess of the god Nanna in Ur, and the priest of the goddess Inanna in Uruk.
note: Appointments recorded in year names.

quote: Lipit-Ištar (1927–1917 BCE), son of Išme-Dagān, used in his royal inscriptions the same titles as his father, but in addition, he referred to himself as “the king who established justice in the land of Sumer and Akkad.” This statement must refer to the collection of laws issued by Lipit-Ištar.
note: Stone stele fragments and about thirteen school copies; the format follows the Laws of Ur-Namma (p. 137).

quote: I, Lipit-Ištar, son of the god Enlil, obligated those in a household of a living father and in an undivided household of brothers to service for seventy (days per year). I obligated those in a household of dependent workers to service for ten days per month.
note: Prologue of the Laws of Lipit-Ištar. Išme-Dagān exempted Nippur from taxes (p. 134); Enlil-bāni’s year 2 annuls taxes and service duties in Isin (p. 140).

quote: Interestingly, in the reign of Būr-Sîn, documents were dated not only by the king’s official year names but also by counting his regnal years by number, at least from his 9th to his 20th regnal year. This method of dating would be abandoned under Būr-Sîn’s successors.
note: Royal dating is imposed on documents, but the experiment lapses.

quote: The need for Erra-imittī to fight against those cities and destroy them indicates that the territory of the kingdom of Isin had shrunk considerably by the time he rose to the throne.
note: Kisurra and Kazallu, 20 to 100 km from Isin.

quote: Only towards the end of the 20th century BC do larger groups of letters begin to appear – first the thousands of mostly private and business-oriented communications of the Assyrian merchants from Kārum Kaniš in Anatolia, and then the 18th century royal correspondence from the age of Hammurapi of Babylon and Yasma-Addu and Zimrilim of Mari.
note: Before c. 1850 royal correspondence is scarce; the large royal archives belong to the Old Babylonian row.
archive: Kaneš merchant houses; Mari palace; Larsa crown

quote: The kings of Isin claimed the political inheritance of Ur, and the scribes of their administration emulated the previous tradition.
The kings of Larsa installed there one of their daughters as high priestess (entum) of the god Sin, thus continuing a tradition going back to the period of Akkad.
note: Ur under Larsa from 1925.

quote: The bureaucratic centralism of the Ur III Period gave way to an economy more conducive to private initiative. Some dynasties of merchants amassed considerable wealth, a phenomenon documented by the numerous family archives found in Babylonian cities.
note: Larsa real-estate boom c. 1800 (Old Babylonian row).

quote: the empire’s rulers and subjects inhabited public and private worlds that were comprehensively marked by this new era-time. Three case studies—of fiscality (taxes, archives, and their authorizing procedures), trade (coinage, weights and measures, and the agora), and imperial communications—demonstrate how the Seleucid temporal regime could model administrative procedures and penetrate deep into social life.
note: The Seleucid Era: a continuous imperial count from 311 BCE, used in Babylonian tablets. Only the introduction is in the folder.

quote: le témoignage de la documentation cunéiforme y est complété par l’apport de quelque 14 450 timbres fiscaux estampillés sur des bullae et cretulae d’argile mises au jour dans la région, qui portent en général une courte inscription grecque accompagnée d’une date
note: Over 99% from the archive building of Seleucia-on-the-Tigris; taxes in kind, in silver and service (§§ 1.1-1.3). The documents they sealed (on parchment) are lost.

quote: Le iiie s. séleucide semble donc avoir été marqué par une intégration pleine et entière de la Babylonie à l’espace monétaire séleucide. Celle-ci se caractérisa par l’abandon du système monétaire mixte au profit d’une production unifiée de monnayages royaux d’étalon attique
note: Turning point under Antiochus I (281-261).

quote: Les Séleucides semblent en effet avoir ménagé une place bien plus importante aux communautés locales, en s’appuyant sur la notabilité liée aux sanctuaires suméro-akkadiens pour l’administration des villes anciennes
note: Crown sustained these local intermediaries by land grants, benefactions and tax exemptions.

quote: la Couronne devait assurer la viabilité économique de ces relais locaux par des donations foncières, des actions évergétiques ou des exemptions fiscales
note: Temples as local partners of the crown rather than state units.

quote: it is an Akkadian translation of a collection of Greek official documents issued by the Seleucid administration in the first quarter of the third century BC, concerning the rebuilding of the Bīt Rēš
note: Royal letters reached the Uruk temple authorities in Greek; the Greek parchment originals are lost.

quote: Kidin-Anu also acted as “Elder Brother” (ahu rabû) of the Bīt Rēš, the temple’s most prominent sacerdotal position at the time, which probably explains why he was both the head of the city’s assembly and the main local interlocutor of the Seleucid administration, just like the high administrator (šatammu) of the Esagil temple in Babylon.
note: Local temple elites as the crown’s intermediaries.

quote: YOS 20, 87 indisputably shows an active support from the Crown, which enabled the Urukean authorities to organize a cultic refoundation in the Bīt Rēš
note: Alexander "revived the old Sumero-Akkadian custom of royal patronage over the temples"; royal patronage rather than state management.

quote: Benché documentino l’attività, nel mercato delle prebende, di individui che richiamano per lo più la propria appartenenza a pochi tra i grandi clan della Uruk del tempo, si tratta di documenti emananti dal tempio e dunque di natura ufficiale piuttosto che privata.
note: Following Beaulieu 1989. Same page describes the tablets: about 1 cm thick, "di forma quadrangolare bombata (circa 10-12 centimetri per lato)", sealed on all four edges. Corpus: 536 archival texts from Seleucid Uruk (Doty).

quote: L’isqu ha decisamente assunto tutte le caratteristiche della proprietà privata: è soggetta a compravendita e locazione, può costituire corredo dotale e sembra divenire appannaggio di un ceto sociale specifico.
note: Prebends "nelle mani di poche famiglie".

quote: The Seleucids ruled over a great part of this landscape of “Asia,” depositing their evidentiary trace, for almost two and a half centuries. The diversity and size of the empire and its neighbors and the patchiness of source survival have rendered its political history both byzantine and dispiritingly lacunose.
note: Empire organised in satrapies (Babylonia, Susiane, the "Upper Satrapies").

quote: Other families seem, in the same way, to have specialized in particular professions. For example, the descendants of Ekur-zakir were often exorcists and sometimes also astrologers. Many descendants of Ah’utu held administrative responsibilities in the temple and sometimes also the city. There is a strong correlation between specific families and the area of their professional expertise (Doty 1977).
note: Cuneiform learning transmitted in temple-linked families; tablet collections in private houses (p. 755). [Rescored by ShG, 8 Nov, from 1 to 2.]

quote: Civil judicial courts had to be able to use the documents.
note: Leather (alphabetic) originals required before royal courts; cuneiform clay copies valid before the temple court.

quote: To conclude, there was a clear hierarchy in the writing media used in Hellenistic Uruk. From a legal perspective, the most important medium was leather, inscribed in alphabetic script, as it was readable and acceptable to the Greek authorities and moreover difficult to corrupt.
note: Cuneiform clay restricted to the temple community; state bureaucracy wrote on leather.

quote: The temples also owned sizeable cattle herds and large parcels of fields around Uruk and in other parts of Babylonia.
from the reign of Antiochus I, especially in the case of some taxed transactions, contracts on clay tablets were superseded by contracts written on folded parchment sealed by bullae.
note: n. 24, after Doty 1977 p. 323: Antiochus I’s tax on slave sales moves such contracts from cuneiform tablets to parchment. A salt-tax registry stamp appears on sealings from Seleucia (p. 183).

quote: With regard to the impressions of official seals, this seems to confirm that officers of the Seleucid administration may have been in charge in both cities
note: The same official seals at Uruk and Seleucia on the Tigris.

quote: so we may infer that the sealers of the bullae, too, may have been witnesses and that these lost folded documents from Seleucia sealed by bullae may have concerned tax-exempt transactions between private subjects.
note: Inference from shared witness seals.

quote: There are clear indications that both of these states invested in establishing an infrastructure, albeit of limited scope, that would enable regular long-distance communications across difficult terrain. Envoys, who held considerable social and political status and personal clout, were the preferred way to communicate long-distance, with written messages playing only a secondary role.
note: New Kingdom Egypt and the Hittite state; about 500 letters from Šapinuwa and 97 from Tapikka.

quote: Like New Kingdom Egypt, the Hittite state relied on a mix of writing media and, to a lesser degree, various languages and scripts, with little in the way of standardization.
note: "no concerted effort to archive the state correspondence systematically" (Weeden, ch. 2).

quote: If we assume a world of bookkeeping and socio-economic and legal administration as well as of private records, we may reach a kind of false equilibrium
note: Van den Hout argues that the absence of private and bookkeeping records should be taken seriously rather than filled by hypothetical wooden tablets ("Mesopotamia light").

quote: These wooden tablets are often adduced as a kind of deus ex machina to explain the absence of sources that we would like to see (e.g., bookkeeping, contracts, and legal and socio-economic records in general) but that are not there.
note: Administration largely without cuneiform bookkeeping; contrast scholars who posit wooden boards with hieroglyphs.

quote: Only once is a local é.dub.ba.a attested in a letter written to Maşat Höyük ... Is that really enough to postulate a scribal school as an institution as it was known in the Ur III and Old Babylonian Periods?
note: Torri: the House on the Slope partly a school; Weeden: Hattuša scribal school "either extremely small, or very disciplined and conservative" (p. 49). Cites Gordin 2015.

quote: the internal territories were organized into governorships of various sizes under Provincial Governors and Frontier Governors ... Distribution of the territories to royal princes can be described as a feudal organization on the one hand, but the state was also highly centralized on the other.
note: Appanage kingdoms (Karkamiš, Aleppo, Tarhuntašša) under cadet lines of the royal family.

quote: Contrary to what would be expected from a bureaucracy, the high offices of the administration lack a rationally established hierarchy; they do not possess well defined spheres of responsibilities; and examples of training, regulation, fixed amounts of compensation, and regular promotions are far too few
note: A Weberian patrimonial organization; the Maşat letters show the king’s "micro-management".

quote: The extent of the royal family’s involvement at all levels of the organization was considerable. Beside the territorial administration that was entirely in the hands of the royal family members, offices of the central administration were also largely occupied by those who were identified by princely designations.
note: Palace and royal family as the organising institution; nearly 40% of high officials after Šuppiluliuma I were "princes".

quote: Law cannot exist without authority to impose and execute it. In the judicial sphere the authority of the king expressed itself in his role as supreme judge.
note: Law collection with royal court cases ("court of the king", "gate of the palace"); reforms replace corporal punishment with fines (pp. 6-7).

quote: Beneath him various officials were charged with administering justice: the provincial governors (Akk. bēl madgalti Hitt. auriyas isḫas) and the dignitaries / magistrates
note: Governor sits with local elders as representative of the central government.

quote: But at least we see from CTH 269 that the central government intervened to alter the prices of commodities
note: Laws §§ 176-186 give standard prices (pp. 220-221; "This is the tariff ... for the city (Hattusa)").

quote: There are also several attestations of EN KUR-TI that appear in the context of tax and corvée obligations (šahhan and luzzi). These attestations often come from land donation documents where exemptions from such obligations are indicated.
note: Governors and town commissioners as authorities to whom dues are owed.

quote: In HKM 52:10–18, Hattušili demands that Himuili improve the conditions of a “House of the Scribe” in Tapikka, reminding him that the šahhan and luzzi obligations are not incumbent on scribes, and threatens to report him to the palace.
note: Provincial scribal house under palace protection at Maşat; possible chief scribe (GAL DUB.SAR).

quote: There is no way to know if this specific composition was also used for temples outside the capital, but several other texts like KUB 31.113 (CTH 275.A), KBo 2.4 (CTH 672.D), and KUB 55.21 (CTH 635), indicate that temple personnel in other locations were also subject to similar regulations.
note: CTH 264, royal Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel, binding by oath-like obligations (pp. 373-374).

quote: “Tablet 1 of the obligations of all the temple personnel, of the kitchen personnel of the deities, of the farmers of the deities, and of the cowherds of the deity (and) shepherds of the deity.”
note: Temples with their own farmers and herds; scale not quantified in this source.

quote: When Ḫattušili I (Labarna II) became the sole Hittite king he was already able to raid deeply into the area dominated by Aleppo, destroying Zalbar and Alalaḫ and devastating the territory of Uršum; all this would have been impossible without the control of the Antitaurus region as far as today Maraş and of the Cilician plain.
note: Old Hittite reach in the mid-17th century, before the imperial period.

quote: Telebinu mentions seven towns where the sons of Labarna I were established as princes (DUMU or LÚ), they were all in the territory of the ancient kingdom of Purušḫanda.
note: Old Hittite provincial rule through royal princes (Telipinu Proclamation).

quote: daß sie in kondensierter Form jeweils für ein Jahr über den Gesamtbetrag der vier Arten des gina’u-Opfers aus den Provinzen des assyrischen Reiches informieren, d. h. über die Beträge an Getreide, Honig, Sesam und Früchten.
note: Following Pedersén. Tabular annual lists from the archive of the offering administrators of the Aššur temple; "Die Tafeln weisen in der Regel Querformat auf und sind in fünf Kolumnen eingeteilt."
archive: Assur, Dūr-Katlimmu, Tell Sabi Abyad state archives

quote: Die fünfte nennt die Provinzen bzw. Verwaltungsbezirke des assyrischen Reiches, aus denen das gina’u-Opfer geliefert wurde.
note: The provinces supplied the regular offerings of the Aššur temple; the list may go back to Tukulti-Ninurta I (p. 52).
archive: Assur, Dūr-Katlimmu, Tell Sabi Abyad state archives

quote: Dennoch ist ein Zweifel an der Lückenlosigkeit und Zuverlässigkeit der assyrischen Buchführung grundsätzlich nicht angebracht
note: Only a fraction of the expected receipts survives (about 650 tablets in the archive).

quote: Mit zwei Ausnahmen kehrt ein Grundbestand der aus Tafel VS 21,21 bekannten Toponyme in allen anderen Listen in z. T. festliegender Reihenfolge wieder.
note: 27 provinces in VS 21, 21 (end of Tiglath-pileser I), 15-20 under Ninurta-apil-Ekur. [Rescored by ShG, 8 Nov, from 3 to 2.]

quote: Chapter 9 aims to pull together the evidence for the range and variety of documentation in the ten Middle Assyrian archives, which offer different facets of a single centralised system
note: p. 303 (Dur-Katlimmu): "the well standardised documents provide solid evidence for the palace’s administration of its stock-breeding and agriculture enterprises"; p. 325: standardised plots in several provinces monitored by a qēpu and his scribe.
archive: Assur, Dūr-Katlimmu, Tell Sabi Abyad state archives

quote: The texts from Tell Ali show that the state maintained its own flocks of sheep and goats in other provinces, while the establishment of state-run farms is attested at Tell Chuera.
note: State farms "already in place well before the end of Shalmaneser’s reign, and Durkatlimmu was in no way unique".

quote: Interestingly, the old town of Ṭābetu on the Middle Ḫabur, which had semi-independent status, retained a different calendar with month names which reach back to the Mari period ..., underlining its nominal independence.
note: The Assyrian state used one traditional calendar ("For most of the second millennium, the Assyrians used a traditional calendar with 12 months"), without intercalation (place names normalised from a garbled text layer); the Babylonian calendar was adopted under Tiglath-pileser I or his predecessor (n. 29).

quote: family legal documents predominantly from the 14th century. This largely derives from related families living in Assur, recording their land transactions in villages in the countryside west of the city.
note: Archive M9 (Pedersén); private archives exist alongside the dominant state archives.

quote: Aus dem Fürstentum Assur, das immer wieder in Abhängigkeit zu mächtigeren Nachbarn gerät, wird "Assyrien", māt Aššur. Die spätestens im 13. Jahrhundert voll entwickelte Konzeption des Territorialstaates bildet die ideologische Grundlage für die Entstehung jenes Imperiums
note: Territorial state by the 13th century; expansion into Syria.

quote: Der assyrische Machtbereich ist in Distrikte gegliedert, die von einem Gouverneur (bēl pāhete) geleitet werden. Von dessen Sitz in der Distrikthauptstadt werden administrative Weisungen an die kommunalen Leitungsorgane (hazi’ānu, rab ālāne usw.) weitergegeben.

Für die Zeit des Königs Tukultī-Ninurta I. läßt sich für das Reichsgebiet ein staatlicher Boten- und Kurierdienst nachweisen, dessen Relaisstationen in der Verantwortung der jeweiligen Distriktverwaltungen (bēl pāhete/šaknu, hassihlu) unterhalten werden.
Königliche Bevollmächtigte (qēpūtu) wachen im Namen der Krone über die ordnungsgemäße Abrechnung von Ernteerträgen und kontrollieren deren Bevorratung.

Berufe außerhalb der Landwirtschaft, im besonderen die des Handwerks, sind vor allem in Urkunden der Palast- und Tempelwirtschaft präsent. Es gibt daneben aber deutliche Indizien für eine private handwerkliche Produktion.
note: Large landowners lend grain; progressive pauperisation of free dependants (p. 566). [Rescored by ShG, 8 Nov, from 1 to 2.]

quote: All Middle Assyrian royal scribes were teachers and, more generally, all attested scribal families strove to create Nachwuchs. The case of Marduk-nādin-aḫḫē, royal scribe and scion of a renowned scribal house, cannot have been different: he must have been a teacher and his home must have functioned as a school.
note: Household schooling by royal scribes; Babylonian scholars imported to Assur (pp. 207-215). [Rescored by ShG, 8 Nov, from 1 to 3.]

quote: One of the most striking aspects of Middle Assyrian government style is how different it was from the administrative practices of the Assyrian state in the first millennium.
note: Middle Assyrian bilateral documentation (sealed quasi-legal tablets regulating officials) as a defining feature of the system.

archive: Babylonian family and Murašû archives; Eanna/Ebabbar

note: Uniform terminology spread, but no central collection.
archive: Babylonian family and Murašû archives; Eanna/Ebabbar

note: No empire-wide law code: rules out 3 in its strict sense (law collection AND royal judges AND edicts).

quote: In Babylonia, for example, such royal decrees (dātu ša šarri) can be demonstrated to have stipulated (and at least tentatively unitized) the amount of fiscal and customs obligations, as well as of penalty payments. note: Royal decrees with legal force, applied in Babylonian documents.

In them, a variable number – between three and eight, to be precise – of “royal judges” (dayyānū ša šarri and similar) dispensed justice ... Here, the Achaemenid Great Kings continued a tradition inherited from their Neo‐Babylonian predecessors
note: Royal courts and royal judges, continued from the Neo-Babylonian state.

quote: In the context of this debate, also the absence of an empire‐wide law(‐code) and especially the practice of dispensing justice on the basis of individual cases – under the key word of Einzelfallgerechtigkeit – have been emphasized (e.g. Wiesehöfer 1995; another important critique is Kuhrt 2001).
note: Against Frei's "imperial authorization": justice case by case, no imperial code.

quote: It is well documented that on his initiative all existing laws of Egypt were collected and assembled, probably quite immediately after he reassured Persian rule in Egypt in his third year. note: A royal order to compile a provincial law collection for the imperial administration (Egypt only).

quote: The system of measures appears to correspond to evidence from both Elephantine in Egypt and Persepolis (Naveh and Shaked 2012: p. 37); it is thus indicative of at least some standardization in bookkeeping.
note: The same measures at the two ends of the empire and in the heartland.

quote: Paradoxically, it is not the siglos but the gold series whose weight was based on the shekel standard. By contrast, the silver sigloi maintained the croeseid standard of 5.38 g initially.
note: A royal act aligning the imperial gold coinage with the Mesopotamian shekel; silver kept another standard.

quote: Like the use of Elamite month names instead of transcribed Iranian month names (Hallock 1969: pp. 74–75), and use of Elamite synonyms for Iranian words, some of these choices were geographically conditioned. The Elamite options appear mostly in texts written to the northwest of Persepolis, along the route to Susa
note: Even within the heartland archive the month names were not uniform.

quote: early in the Achaemenid period a fixed 19‐year cycle of intercalation was adopted (Britton 2007) ... After the introduction of the 19‐year cycle, however, responsibility for the administration of the calendar lay with the astronomical experts who were attached to the temples (Steele 2011a).
note: The Babylonian calendar became fixed, but by temple experts, not by royal imposition: a uniform calendar without a royal act.

quote: These functionaries seem to have learned Aramaic as part of their scribal training according to the largely centralized linguistic standard of the Achaemenid chancery, including genre conventions such as the general structure of a letter and the proper forms of address.
note: One chancery standard across provinces (Bactria matches Egypt and the heartland).

quote: These functionaries seem to have learned Aramaic as part of their scribal training according to the largely centralized linguistic standard of the Achaemenid chancery
note: Training of Aramaic chancery scribes to one standard; inferred from the letters ("seem").

note: ShG asked for Young 2024. Cuneiform schooling in Babylonia: shared curriculum, household locus (anchor 1).

quote: Although the members of the Šangi-Ninurta family did not bear any title showing an institutional affiliation, the colophons of their tablets show twice that they nonetheless had access to the collection of the Eanna temple.
note: Household teaching with access to temple holdings: between 1 and 2.

quote: Babylonian temples were the cultic focus and economic centers for their regions. Far from being autonomous, self‐sufficient institutions operating an autarkic redistributive system (as was often assumed), the temples of the sixth and early fifth centuries BCE interacted with and depended on the outside economy.
note: Major institutions of their regions but embedded in a market economy: 2-3.

quote: The main sanctuary was Esagil of Babylon ... which collected taxes from the other temples, ultimately for the benefit of the king, amounting to 3.5% of the agricultural income in the case of the Eanna of Uruk (Jursa 2010: pp. 68–70).
note: Levies on temples for the crown (anchor 2), channelled through Esagil.

As a result of Xerxes’ retaliation against those circles that had supported his contenders for the throne, the leading families in the major Babylonian cities that had staffed the higher echelons of the temples for ages were removed from their offices
note: Control kept or increased, patronage withdrawn; after 484 the crown removed the temple elites.

quote: Babylonian temples were state institutions but traditionally also a focal point of local power, identity, and prestige for the local urban elite. note: State institutions with local elite power: 2-3.

note: Temples in Fārs stand outside the institutional economy the archive records.

quote: This reveals that the central administration worked with prescriptive documentation regulating sacrifices (a cultic calendar, lists of rites on wax boards, etc.; Henkelman 2008: pp. 283–285); that the director could intervene if necessary; that the authorities recognized the principle that the deities to receive state‐sponsored worship were simply those belonging to the place in question.
note: In the heartland, cult was provisioned and regulated by the state administration.

quote: The same traditional system is found at Persepolis more than a century later: The PFA describes a centralized (yet not all‐embracing) institutional economy under directorship of Parnakka. It had thousands of dependent workers known as kurtaš
note: The crown's institutional economy dominates the heartland record ("not all-embracing").

quote: In size, the territory of the Persepolis institutional economy roughly matches that of modern‐day Switzerland. This comparison also underlines the vertical organization of the landscape ... Lower valleys and larger intermontane plains were fully integrated in the institutional sphere. Higher altitudes, especially fit for summer pasture, fell outside
note: Scale of the royal economy in Fārs.

quote: What limited and mostly indirect evidence we have for royal domain land indicates that they, too, were an important source of income for the crown. note: In Babylonia the crown's own estates were minor; its weight came through taxation, not a palace economy.

quote: The central element of this system were land allotments (e.g. bīt qašti bow properties) granted by the crown or its representatives to numerous individuals or to a group of individuals (organized in kiṣru or hadru collectives) in return for a form of military service (Van Driel 2002: pp. 226–273).
note: Land-for-service system, organized in collectives under crown officials.

quote: In contrast to Herodotus’ assessment, money taxes directly paid to the crown do not seem to have been the principal means by which the Persians exploited the resources of Babylonia. Instead, we see a system that was primarily geared toward the mobilization of workers and soldiers.
note: Qualifies the Herodotean picture of a monetary tribute list: heavy, but labour and service rather than an integrated money tax.

quote: Use of the word data is evidence for the distinctive importance of something we can call ‘law’ in the interaction between imperial ruler and subjects. ... It is my contention that, among the characteristics of that stable situation, a significant and distinctive one is the rule of law.
note: Tuplin calls his own argument "cumulative and impressionistic": royal law (data) as a hallmark of the empire, without an empire-wide code.

quote: In Babylonia, where the (much more extensive) documentation is of a different character, the few Iranian-named judges are a decided minority ... and even people with special titles such as ‘royal judge’, ‘judge of the palace-gate’ and databara or ‘judge of Gubaru or Artareme’ can have Babylonian names. (Babylonian-named judges even appear in Susa — a sign that the legal norms in use reflect the identity of the litigants and locus delicti, not the location of the process
note: Royal judicial titles exist, but the law applied followed the litigants (local law), not an imperial norm.

quote: When some time after Euagoras’ death (374 BCE) Phoenicia and Cyprus revolted, both were subdued a few years later in 345 BCE. Nonetheless, the Great King Artaxerxes III did not replace indirect rule by direct administration.
note: City kings remain under Persian supremacy: the empire tolerates indirect rule at its edges.

quote: Achaemenid Anatolia was a place where imperial authority could be and was expressed powerfully, but it was also a place where individuals exercised autonomy, mostly in ways that allowed them to express their individual identity within the rubric of administrative authority.
note: Satrapal authority with local autonomy.

quote: Questo potrebbe essere un altro indizio a conferma dell’ipotesi di una possibile struttura socio-politica che unisse, all’epoca degli archivi di Fara, almeno una parte della Mesopotamia.

quote: una « ristrutturazione di parte dei territori agricoli delle città di Adab, Umma e Lagash, in seguito alla creazione di una nuova unità amministrativa con centro ad ‘Unken’, sotto la giurisdizione di Lagash »
note: One city given jurisdiction over a unit formed from the land of others (Pettinato's reading, endorsed by Visicato).

quote: Ur-Namma schafft schließlich eine gültige Rechtsordnung, die in seinem "Codex Ur-Namma" niedergelegt ist, die älteste bekannte altorientalische Gesetzessammlung.

quote: Und wie ist Datum S 21 zu verstehen, das von einer Reformierung des Tempellandes von Enlil und Ninlil zu sprechen scheint: werden damit alle Tempel dem König unterstellt, wie man dies allgemein annimmt? ... Eine Frage, die wir wohl aufgrund der dürftigen Urkundenlage nicht beantworten können; ein markanter Unterschied scheint sich jedoch für den Süden des Landes nicht anzudeuten.
note: The supposed royal takeover of temple land under Šulgi is not visible in the southern archives.

quote: Viele wichtige Ämter des Reiches sind regional gebunden: ensi2 und zum Teil šagina an die Provinz, sanga und šabra an den Tempel, hazannum an die Ortschaft, jeweils sind ihnen untergebene Verwaltungsstrukturen zugeordnet. Daneben existiert eine königlich-staatliche Administration
note: Temple households keep their own administration inside the provincial system.

quote: The military activities of the Ur III kings to the east and north-east of their frontier were undertaken to ensure the continued flow of this tribute, both from dependent states and from military personnel and high-ranking officials of the kingdom. Significantly, these were raids aimed at securing resources and weakening outside groups; they were not aimed at the outright control of foreign territory.
note: A core of provinces with a tributary periphery, not annexation.

quote: Kernland und Peripherie des Ur III-Reiches (nach P. Steinkeller, SAOC 46)
note: The map of core, periphery and vassal states follows Steinkeller 1987.

quote: C'est à Nippur que la continuité est la plus complète, puisqu'il n'y a pas de rupture dans les archives du temple d'Inanna. Apparemment, rien n'a changé dans le pays de Sumer et d'Akkad, sinon que le siège du pouvoir s'est déplacé d'Ur à Isin, selon la volonté divine: c'est du moins l'idéologie que les souverains d'Isin s'efforcèrent de répandre
note: Isin keeps Ur III record-keeping; continuity is also an ideological claim.

quote: Le souverain est «pourvoyeur de Nippur», le roi d'Isin étant responsable de l'approvisionnement des temples de cette ville.
note: Under Išme-Dagan; his daughter Enanatuma installed as entum at Ur.

quote: Les temples semblent avoir été moins sensibles aux aléas de la vie politico-militaire, puisqu'ils ont dans certains cas conservé leurs textes administratifs sur une durée plus longue. Ainsi, les archives du temple de Ninurta à Nippur (l'Ešumeša) s'étendent sur plus de 75 ans ... celles du magasin du temple de Ningal à Ur (le Ganunmah), couvrent 120 années
note: Temple economies outlast changes of ruler.

quote: Ešnunna ... était à l'époque de la troisième dynastie d'Ur le siège d'un gouverneur (ensi). Lorsque le royaume d'Ur se décomposa sous Ibbi-Sîn, Šu-iliya, fils du gouverneur Ituriya, se proclama roi à Ešnunna
note: Former Ur III governors become kings: the provincial hierarchy dissolves into city-states.
archive: Ešnunna (Šu-Sin temple and Palace of the Rulers)

quote: Ur-Ninurta se proclama «pasteur d'Ur», alors qu'il put seulement envoyer des offrandes au temple de Ningal en l'an 9 et 13 de Gungunum. Bur-Sin (1897-1876) porta le titre de «puissant fermier d'Ur»; il est vrai qu'il reprit le contrôle sur Ur, mais il le perdit rapidement
note: Titles claim more territory than the kings held.

quote: Outre un certain nombre de lettres qui lui furent adressées, on a retrouvé de nombreux textes administratifs dans le palais, encore inédits
note: Royal letters exist at Ešnunna (Bilalama) and Isin (Lipit-Eštar and his general Nanna-kiag, p. 84), but in small numbers.

quote: Il s'agit de lettres en sumérien dont les rois d'Isin sont les expéditeurs ou les destinataires; elles ne sont connues que par des copies plus tardives, effectuées dans des écoles à titre d'exercice
note: The Isin royal correspondence survives only as later school copies; its authenticity is debated.

quote: tous les royaumes n'ajoutaient pas de mois intercalaires au même moment, d'où des décalages entre les calendriers des différents royaumes. À la fin de chaque année, la chancellerie faisait parvenir aux différentes villes de province une tablette comportant le nom de la nouvelle année.
note: Year names are standard within each kingdom, but each kingdom keeps its own calendar.

quote: au point que de véritables plagiats ont pu être constatés dans le cas de certains hymnes d'Išme-Dagan, décalquant ceux de Šulgi
note: The Isin court continues Ur III scholarly production; direct evidence for schools of this period is thin.
archive: Isin royal hymns; later school copies

quote: On doit mentionner en premier lieu la promulgation d'un «Code de lois», que rappellent presque toutes les inscriptions commémoratives de ce souverain, à commencer par celle consacrée à la construction de la «Maison de la Justice» (é ni-si-sá).
note: Lipit-Eštar of Isin. Charpin adds that these aspects "pourraient faire illusion": the kingdom was already losing ground to Larsa.

quote: Le «Code» du roi d'Isin Lipit-Eštar, le plus ancien, fut rédigé en sumérien. ... Alors que le Code de Lipit-Eštar et les Lois d'Ešnunna ne sont connus que par des copies sur tablettes
note: The oldest of the three Old Babylonian law collections; known from tablet copies only.

quote: Du moins observe-t-on qu'Išme-Dagan exempta Nippur de son tribut et ses habitants du service militaire
note: An exemption presupposes a royal levy of tribute and military service on the cities of the kingdom.

quote: À l’époque hellénistique, les biens de la Couronne étaient gérés par un organisme que les sources cunéiformes désignent par le nom de bīt šarri (litt. « maison du roi »), dans lequel les assyriologues s’accordent à reconnaître le basilikon des sources grecques. Cette institution remplissait également d’autres fonctions liées à l’évergétisme royal et au contrôle des activités des sanctuaires.
note: A royal economic office (basilikon) managing crown property and supervising the temples.

quote: La documentation cunéiforme ne permet pas de déterminer l’étendue des domaines royaux séleucides dans la région.
note: The size of the royal domain is unknown; the surviving archives are temple archives.

quote: l’appui aux communautés urbaines anciennes (villes suméro-akkadiennes) et nouvelles (poleis), qui s’est traduit au cours du iiie s. par une politique de dévolution foncière destinée à s’assurer la collaboration politique de ces communautés à l’échelle locale. Les sources ne permettent pas d’estimer la part du domaine royal concernée par ces dévolutions, mais plusieurs indices portent à croire qu’elle ne fut pas négligeable
note: The crown gave away royal land to cities and temples: the palace sector is large but not dominant.

quote: Cette institution remplissait également d’autres fonctions liées à l’évergétisme royal et au contrôle des activités des sanctuaires.
note: The royal bīt šarri supervised temple activity.

quote: C’est le šatammu qui représentait la ville auprès des rois assyriens, puis achéménides, séleucides et parthes, c’est-à-dire lorsqu’il n’y avait pas de pouvoir royal babylonien autonome. Il apparaît que ses responsabilités s’étendaient à une assez vaste région en dehors de Babylone. ... Les šatammu se succédaient de manière héréditaire
note: The temple head was hereditary, not a royal appointee, and spoke for the city to the king: temples as partners, not units of the state.

quote: the many references to official orders (ṭēmu, ll. 4, 11, 19, 36, 37 and 39) and/or royal letters (l. 13) recorded over more than fifteen years for the sole refoundation of the Bīt Rēš, show an actual involvement from the first Seleucids in this kind of euergetism
note: Royal orders over fifteen years steer one temple refoundation.

quote: À la fois lieux de culte, grands propriétaires terriens, conservatoires de la culture suméro-akkadienne et relais politiques du pouvoir royal, les sanctuaires occupaient une place essentielle dans le paysage institutionnel de la Babylonie hellénistique.
Nous ne disposons pas, pour l’époque hellénistique, d’une documentation suffisante pour évaluer le rôle joué par les sanctuaires dans l’économie locale.
note: Monerie warns that in the sixth century the temples depended on crown subsidies (p. 285), and the Hellenistic evidence cannot show more.

quote: S’y ajoutaient de nombreux documents inscrits en grec ou en araméen sur peau ou (plus rarement) sur papyrus, qui avaient valeur légale devant les autorités royales. L’emploi de ces documents sur support souple était si répandu que les temples entretenaient un corps permanent de scribes spécialisés, appelés sepīrū, pour les produire.
note: A royal administration in Greek and Aramaic on leather, which the temples had to serve with their own scribes.

quote: le témoignage de la documentation cunéiforme y est complété par l’apport de quelque 14 450 timbres fiscaux estampillés sur des bullae et cretulae d’argile mises au jour dans la région ... plus de 99 % de ces empreintes de sceaux fiscaux ont été mises au jour dans le bâtiment des archives de Séleucie-du-Tigre.
note: A central record office at the royal capital: a bureaucracy on perishable media, seen only through its sealings.

quote: Inscribed royal letters, issued in a recognizable chancery style by the Seleucid court or its agents, delivered instructions, appointed officials, established cults, and bestowed benefactions. These letters, sometimes inscribed alongside the forwarding notes of subordinates, provide crucial information for the titles, terminology, and hierarchical organization of the imperial administration.
note: A chancery and a written chain of command (empire-wide, mainly the west).

quote: Cuneiform sources from Northern Babylonia such as the astronomical diaries and the chronicles regularly mention the reception of leather documents (kuššipištu) sent to local authorities by the royal chancery
note: Regular royal written orders reach the Babylonian cities.

quote: Seleucid roadways and road infrastructure are of major importance as the material manifestation of royal movements, as instruments of territorial integration, and as a disciplinary mechanism for bodies and space. Our evidence for Seleucid “Royal Roads” is, inevitably, uneven and scant, but it is intriguing.
note: Royal roads exist, but the evidence is thin.

quote: “Trafficflow” maps of all known royal journeys identify the directionality and frequency of the kings’ movement and the practical and ideological significance of Royal Roads. It is shown that royal mobility was the major mechanism of provincial integration
note: Integration through the moving court rather than a fixed relay system.

quote: These letters, sometimes inscribed alongside the forwarding notes of subordinates, provide crucial information for the titles, terminology, and hierarchical organization of the imperial administration.
Par ailleurs, l’imposition de service (ilku) aux propriétaires fonciers et les systèmes de dépendance rurale semblent avoir été repris à leur compte par les souverains séleucides.
note: Service dues on land kept from the Achaemenid system.

quote: Le cas déjà mentionné de la taxation des ventes d’esclaves et de terres arables par l’administration séleucide à partir du milieu des années 270, qui entraîna l’enregistrement de ces
note: A royal sales tax that changed how contracts were written (see also Messina 2009 p. 179).

quote: By contrast, time according to the Seleucid Era, decoupled from the death-accession cycle, was transformed from being concrete, immanent, and process linked into being abstract, homogeneous, and transcendent. ... This little-heralded achievement was a highly politicized act. The Seleucid Era established the chronological backbone along which the kingdom’s
note: A royal dating system for the whole empire (with the Attic coin standard, Monerie 2017 p. 276).

quote: la plupart des monnayages d’argent qui circulaient en Basse-Mésopotamie dans la seconde moitié du Ier millénaire av. J.-C. étaient frappés selon un étalon différent de l’étalon babylonien.
note: Local weighing of silver against a foreign coin standard lasted into the early Hellenistic period.

quote: Dynastic strife and Timarchus’ revolt had fatally eroded Seleucid authority in the Upper Satrapies: under Mithridates I, the Parthian kingdom had expanded from the Caspian region to occupy Media in 148/7, Babylonia in 141, and Elymaïs in 140.
note: Chronology: Babylonia is a Seleucid province 311-141 BC; after 141 it is Parthian (outside this period).

quote: Antiochus III also reasserted Seleucid dominance in the Upper Satrapies. In 220 he defeated Molon, the rebellious satrap of Media, and imposed suzerainty on Artabazanes, the ruler of Media Atropatene.
note: Revolts of satraps and reconquest: wide reach, but contested at the edges.

quote: S’y ajoutaient de nombreux documents inscrits en grec ou en araméen sur peau ou (plus rarement) sur papyrus, qui avaient valeur légale devant les autorités royales.
note: Royal authorities judge on documents in Greek; no royal law collection is known.

quote: L’usage de ces documents, déjà fréquent au début du Ier millénaire av. J.-C., semble s’être répandu au cours des siècles, ce dont témoigne en négatif la réduction du spectre des activité documentées par les textes cunéiformes, qui apparaît beaucoup moins large à l’époque hellénistique qu’au vie s. av. J.-C.
note: Private business moved to parchment; the cuneiform record under-reports it.

quote: A big part of the tablets found in Ue XVIII was the product of scribal training for pupils who studied Akkadian and Sumerian scholarly series in order to specialise in the art of the healer at a later stage. Various phases of the school curriculum are evident in the assemblage, highlighting the domestic context of apprenticeship.
note: Training in the house of a healer family.

quote: Several tablets from his collection were written as a part of the scribal training of his son Ištar-šum-ēreš, but also of a certain Anu‑ab-uṣur, descendant of the Kurî family, and maybe of Anu-ab-uṣur, descendant of the Gimil-Anu family. Both the Kurî and Gimil-Anu families belonged to the traditional Urukean urban elite.
note: Household teaching took in pupils from other temple families: a shared curriculum, not yet an institution.

quote: Les tablettes étaient régulièrement recopiées, pour l’apprentissage des scribes, pour la conservation des écrits ou encore pour la constitution de collections. ... la relation du copiste au propriétaire qui est très souvent familiale, le fils copiant pour le père.
note: Colophons show training within the family.

quote: The cuneiform evidence indicates that a royal tax on the sale of slaves (andrapodon) and a general sales tax (eponion) were imposed early in the reign of Antiochus I Soter (ca. 274 B.C.). ... After the imposition of these taxes all sale documents involving slaves or arable land had to be written on papyrus or parchment, rather than cuneiform tablets, and registered with the Seleucid royal notary officer (chreophylax).
note: A royal registry for private sales: the state bureaucracy now writes in Greek on perishable media (chapter IV, pp. 308ff.).

quote: During the early Old Kingdom, the state was made up of small provinces, each centered around an important settlement of the time and ruled by Hittite princes. Our sources from this period are too scarce to determine how centralized or feudal this structure was.
note: Old Kingdom: princes in small provinces; degree of central control unknown.

quote: Starting with the early Empire period, following the permanent integration of Kizzuwatna into the Hittite domain, we see the first instances of the installation of princes as appanage kings. This continued with the expansion into northern Syria ... In the meantime the internal territories were organized into governorships of various sizes under Provincial Governors and Frontier Governors.
note: Empire: appanage kingdoms and graded governorships.

quote: In terms of changes in these administrative offices, no particular period of Hittite history may be recognized as a time of radical transformation. Instead the changes seem to have taken place gradually throughout the state’s existence. Growth in number of offices more or less parallels the growth of the state into an empire
note: No single break: offices grow gradually with the territory.

quote: During the early Old Kingdom, the state was made up of small provinces, each centered around an important settlement of the time and ruled by Hittite princes.
note: Old Kingdom: a central Anatolian state.

quote: Distribution of the territories to royal princes can be described as a feudal organization on the one hand, but the state was also highly centralized on the other. While the appanage kings had their own territorial responsibilities, they were often called to the assistance of the Great King
note: Empire: Anatolia and northern Syria under one king.

quote: The second part of King Telipinu’s proclamation of the late sixteenth century bc documents a network of over ninety storehouses for grain throughout Central Anatolia ... on the archaeological side, the silos in Hattusa and provincial centers are an eloquent testament to the Hittite state seeking to guarantee a regular and steady ﬂow of foodstuffs.
note: A royal storage network across the core.

quote: The storage facilities mentioned in the Telipinu text cover the core of Hatti-Land as well as the Upper and Lower Land and bespeak a ﬁne-grained and therefore also highly localized or decentralized system of local networks that together form the Hittite kingdom. Within such a system it is possible to work without written records to a large extent.
note: The palace economy ran through local networks, largely without records.

quote: There were several regional palaces which not only served as administrative institutions but also acted as royal residences during the visits of the king.

Given the general attitude to incorporate and support such local religious traditions, regular inspections were carried out. These were laid down in written reports known as cult inventories ... cult inventories were reports drawn up town by town. These were purely administrative records whose life expired once the next inspection came around or when the changes ordained from the capital on receiving the report had been implemented.
note: The capital inspected and reordered local cults, town by town.

quote: the passage from the Instruction of the Temple Personnel ... offers the perfect example for the control the palace tried to exert on the distribution of wealth and possible related record keeping: If by the palace silver, gold, textiles, (and/or) things of bronze are given to him (i.e., a member of the temple personnel) as a gift, it should be speciﬁed: “King so-and-so has given it to him” and it should likewise be recorded how much its weight is.
note: Royal instructions regulate temple staff.

quote: Given the general attitude to incorporate and support such local religious traditions, regular inspections were carried out.
note: Local temples depend on royal support and inspection rather than running an economy of their own.

quote: In order to avoid this, the state invested in mobilizing the staples and organizing them at a local level and thus tried to provide for the inevitable lean years.
note: Levies in kind stored locally.

quote: In the tribute (MANDATTU) inventory text KUB 26.66 with dupl. KBo 18.153 rev. 15, two minas of silver held by Walwaziti and Pupuli are said to have been previously taken up by the queen.
note: Tribute inventories at the capital.

quote: KUB 42.66 rev. 4'–6' refers to weight?-stones (stamped) with the seal of the queen
note: Weights sealed by the queen: a palace standard (one text).

quote: It makes reference to standard weights and scales, as well as bribery, but the context is too damaged to obtain a clear understanding.

Dating of letters by historical criteria is often impossible. Although royal senders or receivers are indicated by name in the diplomatic correspondence, in the internal correspondence the king and queen are not identified by name. ... Hagenbuchner (1989a, 106) cites KBo 28.66, KBo 18.59, and KUB 3.80 as rare examples of letters that gives their dates.
note: No dating system in administrative writing: rules out STD 3 (measures and dating).

quote: The texts recovered from the Hittite capital city, Ḫattuša, as well as from the three provincial centers that have yielded an appreciable number of tablets (Tapikka [Maşat Höyük], Šapinuwa [Ortaköy near Çorum], and Šarišša [Kuşaklı]), represent official correspondence carried on in the course of administrating the business of the king.
note: Royal letters reach provincial centres.

quote: In all instruction and oath texts, the king demands the direct loyalty of all of his nobles and high officials to himself alone, with no intervening layers of administration. The Maşat letters are particularly demonstrative of the micro-management of the Hittite king regarding various trivial matters.
Travel in winter within Anatolia was extremely slow and hazardous, and was avoided when possible. ... But the presence of ice and snow on the roads was always a reason not to travel
note: Seasonal limits on communication.

quote: Unfortunately, what private, unofficial letter writing went on has left no examples.
note: Silent record: absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

quote: Finally, there is the near-total silence of the Hittite sources on trade.
note: Silent record.

quote: Reforms and Modifications of the Laws. The following diachronic stages in the formulation of Hittite law can be distinguished.
note: The collection was revised by the crown from the Old to the New Hittite manuscripts.

quote: they oversaw the judicial activities of their local vassals, but were frequently in need of the Great King’s intervention
note: Royal justice exists but depends on the king in person.

quote: the suspicion that it would have been sealed and enclosed in an envelope is confirmed by a letter from the king found at Durkatlimmu in which he writes "I have sent a directive to Adaya, (and) I have sealed the envelope and the tablet with my seals"
note: Sealed royal directives reach a provincial centre on the Habur.

quote: Royal commands (abat sarri) could come in a letter authenticated by a royal seal, and the word sipirtu ... is employed for requests brought by messenger from a different sector of the administration.
note: Written royal orders beside oral messages.

quote: one of the chancellors serving the king, the city scribe, the herald and the king's representatives shall be present. The person who is acquiring the village, the field or the house, the mayor (and) three elders of the village shall be present, shall have the herald proclaim
note: Land transfer under royal officials, with tablets written for the judges.

quote: in §§ 17-18 we read that a dissatisfied farmer could secure a written order from judges to authorise his use of water resources

Whether the official calendar had a year of 354 or of 360 days, there is no sign in the Middle Assyrian calendar of the intercalary months which had been used for centuries in Babylonia to adjust the lunar to the solar year
note: One official calendar and eponym dating; the Babylonian calendar was adopted under Tiglath-pileser I or Aššur-rēša-iši (n. 29): a turning-point candidate.

quote: a payment made on the instruction of (ina sipirti) an official outside the temple (Col. F: in Nos. 9 and 19 the Governor of the Land (i.e. Assur province); in No. 31 another provincial governor)
note: The temple's offerings office acts on governors' orders and lends to palace officials.

quote: The "debtors" include a palace overseer (No. 23), the mayors of Sudugi (No. 7) and Kilizi (No. 31), a priest of Adad (No. 14), a palace scribe (No. 16), boatmen (Nos. 1; 20), a diviner (No. 22), a provincial governor (No. 29) and the Governor of the Land (No. 30).
note: The Aššur temple's supply is woven into the state system rather than run on its own estates.

quote: In the Middle Assyrian kingdom the position of tupsar sarre "royal scribe" was an elevated one. The title occurs only in the capital, close to the king ... The only function that is actually attested for Middle Assyrian royal scribes is that of teacher.

The evidence indicates that there was never more than one "royal scribe" at a time; occasionally his "son" and student might succeed him (5 to 6), but non-royal scribes trained students too (8), and it was undoubtedly the king who had the final choice.
note: Training in scribal families, with one royal teacher at the top.

quote: werden asû neben einem Beschwörer (āšipu), einem Seher (bārû) und einem Schreiber des Tafelhauses (ṭupšarru ša bēt ṭuppāte) als den bēlē perre zugehörig geführt, die bei der Anlage eines Gartens im Palast von Kār-Tukultī-Ninurta
note: A "scribe of the tablet house" in the royal palace.

quote: Shalmaneser claims to have blinded and taken captive 14,400 people from Hanigalbat after defeating Šattuara, and Tukulti-Ninurta "uprooted" 28,800 "Hittites" from his campaign west of the Euphrates and moved them into "my land". Independent confirmation that such deportations did take place is provided by administrative documents
note: Sequence: Aššur-uballiṭ I independence; Adad-nārārī I and Shalmaneser I take Hanigalbat; Tukultī-Ninurta I west of the Euphrates (Reculeau 2022 already coded).
archive: royal inscriptions; Assur, Tell Chuera and Dur-Katlimmu lists

quote: The sequence according to which these columns were arranged on the tablets seems to be quite strict and standardized, to the point that columns were sometimes inserted even though they were not actually needed and thus left empty.
note: Standard ledger formats in two separate administrative centres (Nippur and Dūr-Enlilē).

quote: an important contribution to the study of centralized administration in Kassite Babylonia is now provided by the Kassite tablets of the Rosen Collection ... they share a number of typological, prosopographical, geographical, and chronological features which make them the second largest coherent set of Middle Babylonian sources after those from Nippur ... “an important economic center that was to a certain degree dependent on Nippur and played an important role in the administration”
note: A second administrative centre tied to Nippur: the bureaucracy was not one city only.

quote: The overwhelming majority of the texts (probably more than ninety percent of those known) come from one site (Nippur) over a restricted period of approximately five generations (c. 1360-1225) and tend to concentrate on the bookkeeping of large economic units there. How full a picture one can create even of these economic units from this documentation is not at all clear
note: Archive bias: one site, five generations.

quote: The first two columns are designated as rēš makkūri (sag níg.ga), and šibšu, which represent respectively the taxable capital and an amount paid on agricultural products that was calculated at a fixed rate upon the taxable capital.
note: A fixed-rate harvest tax, assessed town by town in annual ledgers.

quote: the mechanisms developed by the central administration in order to control and exploit the production of agricultural goods during the Kassite period have been largely neglected in Ancient Near Eastern Studies. This research gap cannot be ascribed to the lack of sources.
There were different vessels used to measure capacities in the Kassite period. For an overview, see Sassmannshausen 2001: 448–49 and Brinkman 2017: 21.
note: Several capacity measures in use side by side.

quote: Die ausgebende Stelle steht in Zusammenhang mit der Palastwirtschaft, denn die Vorderseite der Liste trägt die Überschrift "Gerste, (nach) dem großen sutu-Maß, die von den 10 kurru (3000 qu) ,Entnahme' (massartu) des Palastes gegeben wurde".
note: A palace measure; a temple measure is named elsewhere (p. 40: "dem großen sutu-Maß des Tempels"): institutional, not polity-wide, standards.

quote: tēlītu gišbán gal mu.19.kam Nazi-Maruttaš lugal.e
note: Annual revenue accounts of many towns are headed with the same "large seah" and dated by regnal year in both centres.

quote: bit tuppi "Tontafelhaus, Schule" In einem Brief bekommt der Verwalter Innannu von einer hochgestellten Frau namens Inbi-ajjari folgende Anweisung: "Die Söhne des Tafelhauses (= Schüler) sind dir anvertraut worden. Sorge dauernd für sie!"
note: Pupils of a tablet house entrusted to the chief administrator of the Nippur granary.

quote: Die von Sassmannshausen untersuchten Schülerübungen administrativen Inhalts stammen alle aus Nippur.
note: Exercises in administrative formats: training for the institutional bureaucracy.

quote: Die Tafel 12 N 587 ... wurde zusammen mit einer Gruppe von weiteren, bislang unveröffentlichten Übungstafeln während der 12. Nippur-Kampagne in den Aschegruben eines kassitischen Tempels (WA IV C 9) gefunden.
note: Exercise tablets in a temple context.

quote: dass die dürftige Quellenlage nur eine fragmentarische Bearbeitung beider Themen zulässt
note: Bartelmus warns the evidence on Kassite schooling is thin.

quote: An der Spitze der Gesellschaft im kassitisch beherrschten Babylonien stand der König als Regent, oberster Richter und Heerfiihrer
note: The king as highest judge; no law collection is known for the period.

quote: Eine Gerichtsurkunde, in der es um die Frage geht, ob ein Bauer die šibšu-Abgabe zu leisten hat, und zwei weitere Prozeßurkunden zeigen, daß der "Kanzler" als Richter Gerichtsprozesse entscheiden konnte.
note: Justice by the governor of Nippur.

quote: In der dritten Urkunde ist allerdings schon ein Richter, der den Prozeß entscheidet, genannt. Aus einer Urkunde aus Nippur ist ersichtlich, daß der Bürgermeister auch an Stelle des Richters Gerichtsentscheidungen treffen
note: Local justice by mayors and judges.
